articles.title: Dan Koh, Labor’s Candidate in MA-06, took over $180,000 from AIPAC donors
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: Yard signs for hometown candidate Daniel Koh pepper the gardens of seven-figure homes in Andover, an affluent suburb north of Boston, as the six-way race for the Massachusetts 6th Congressional District enters its final weeks. Koh is dominating the race in campaign cash and endorsements, from labor unions and establishment politicians alike. A Working Mass review found that $180,000 donated to Koh came from donors who had also donated to the American Israel Political Action Committee, or AIPAC. Constituents deserve to know: “Who is paying for all these signs?” Koh’s campaign war chest holds over $4 million according to the most recent FEC filing deadline, more than the rest of the field combined. His campaign is quick to boast that expenditures are largely funded and backed by institutional labor. The Massachusetts AFL-CIO and nearly half of local unions have endorsed Koh, including AFSCME council 93, the International Association of Machinists, NAGE SEIU Local 5000, SEIU Local 888, Teamsters Local 25, UNITE HERE NEJB, the Massachusetts and the Massachusetts Building Trades Union as well as many of its members including, IBEW Local 103, IBEW Local 104, IBEW Local 2222, IUPAT DC 35, Laborers Local 22, Laborers Local 175, Laborers Local 88, and more. I’m proud to stand with labor, and I’m proud to have labor standing with me. Hear directly from labor leaders on why they’re backing our campaign pic.twitter.com/w3Bko5JdAf — Dan Koh (@dank) August 11, 2026 It is likely that many unions see Koh’s frontrunner status as a deterrent to endorsing other challengers. If labor leaders think Koh’s win is inevitable, the incentive to support different, more progressive candidates diminishes. Only a handful of unions have declined to genuflect before him. UAW International and SEIU State Council have backed candidate and State Rep. Tram Nguyen (D-Andover), a member of UAW Local 2320 from past work as a legal aide. The National Education Association and the Massachusetts Teachers Association endorsed candidate Mariah Lancaster. Boston DSA formally recommended against moderate candidates Koh, Nguyen, and financial technology executive John Beccia, but declined to recommend any progressive challenger. For better or worse, Koh is the labor candidate. Given Koh’s resume, this coalition is disappointing, but not surprising. He’s a former protege of Boston’s ‘labor mayor’ Marty Walsh, and served as Mayor Walsh’s chief of staff before following him to the U.S. Department of Labor. Koh also served in the Biden White House, where he was deployed to Michigan to negotiate with the Uncommitted Movement during the presidential primary on the administration’s behalf. There, negotiations were described as “tense,” and Koh and the Biden administration left without conceding any ground in their facilitation of the Gaza genocide. His loyalty earned him the ‘MSNBC trifecta’ endorsements: Former President Joe Biden, Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg. Executives & AIPAC Dollars Labor isn’t the only movement funding Koh. Koh has received criticism for taking the maximum allowable donations from a Palantir executive and from sports gambling websites , among others. According to a review of FEC filings conducted by Working Mass , the Committee to Elect Dan Koh has received at least $183,700 from donors who also gave to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC. Koh has not received funding directly from AIPAC. But at least 68 donors donated to both AIPAC and Dan Koh’s campaign. Their combined donations to AIPAC total $206,395. These donors include Josh Kraft, of the Kraft family, as well as executives at Apollo Asset Management, Bain Capital, and Goldman Sachs. At least 29 of these donors reside out of state, while only five live in the 6th District. Because receipts are only available through the June 30 filing deadline, the total Koh has received is likely larger. The AIPAC-overlapping total is small relative to Koh’s overall haul, but sizable relative to the budgets of his progressive opponents. The $183,700 figure exceeds half of the total campaign funds raised by all of the race’s three progressive challengers, Beth Anders-Beck, Jamie Belsito, and Mariah Lancaster. The donations are a blaring warning signal for the type of Representative Koh intends to be: business as usual, corporate, bland, and likely to continue the technocratic facilitation of extractive and genocidal American wars abroad. The unwitting alliance between labor unions and supporters of America’s most vilified lobbying arm is an indictment of the current state of labor’s electoral orientation: a movement on the defensive, with endorsements rarely democratically decided, and inclined to back establishment figures who prioritize incremental worker concessions over progressive candidates who might shift political leverage from capital to labor. If you’re driving by a yard sign and wondering who paid for it, the answer might be AIPAC-linked donors, a labor union, or both. Tony A is a contributing writer to Working Mass and a resident of Massachusetts’ 6th Congressional District. articles.title: In Peru, Keiko Fujimori Promises Order, Not Reconciliation
articles.author: Rebecca Jarman
articles.content: The polling stations had not long been open when Keiko Fujimori reached the cemetery with her younger sister and her teenage daughters. Dressed uniformly in starch white blouses and blue-wash jeans, they proceeded across the lawn, each carrying a sheaf of roses and carnations. The elder women knelt at their mother’s grave and placed the blush pink flowers in a vase. Heads bowed, they lingered a short while. Then, hand in hand, they walked another twenty paces among the headstones. For her father Alberto, who was Peruvian president from 1990 to 2000, Keiko had brought an arrangement in the national colors of red and white. She led the family in prayer before turning to smile at reporters. Later that day, she cast her vote in a presidential election where, at the fourth time of asking, she won the country’s highest office. Keiko’s visit to her parents’ tombs was a belated response of sorts to Alberto Fujimori’s detractors, who derided a president without any forebears buried in Peruvian soil. Fujimori was merely the son of Japanese migrants when he burst onto the political scene upon his first election in 1990. His surname had no precedent or meaning. Shortly after arriving in Peru in the 1930s, Alberto’s father had adopted a new name. Fujimori translates loosely to “wisteria wood.” It was a fitting choice. He would go on to open a florist business in his adoptive country where Alberto worked as an adolescent, delivering spectacular sculptures on his bicycle to the modernist mansions of Lima. From humble beginnings, Fujimori rose far and fast. Further still he eventually fell, sentenced in 2009 to twenty-five years in prison for human rights abuses and corruption. Now Fujimori bones lie deep in Andean earth. Even so, Keiko’s lineage surely remains controversial. For two generations, Peruvians have followed the elaborate plotlines of dramatic family feuds, beginning with the spat between her father Alberto and her mother Susana Higuchi, who was also part of the Japanese community. Their widely publicized conflict emerged in 1992, when Higuchi accused her husband’s family of misappropriating charitable donations sent from Japan. Keiko first came to public view during their acrimonious divorce: when she was just nineteen, her father, as president, invited her to replace her mother as First Lady. A successful businesswoman and twice member of Congress, Higuchi would aspire to the presidency herself, though her ambitions were extinguished by a vengeful campaign orchestrated by her ex-husband to block her nomination. She retaliated by claiming that she had been tortured on Fujimori’s orders. The tumultuous relationship between Susana and Keiko has long been a subject of speculation. This squabbling has not played out in their favor. Peru is a conservative nation that places great value on integrity and discretion, especially among the elite and the influential. Alberto Fujimori died in 2024, age eighty-six, shortly after his compassionate release from prison. His demise gave Keiko new freedoms in her latest presidential campaign, not least the chance to rewrite her family’s story featuring a reconciliation between her parents on Higuchi’s deathbed. Similar olive branches have, according to Keiko’s staging, been extended among members of the wider family. At Fujimori’s funeral, Keiko embraced her distraught brother, Kenji, whom she had expelled from her Fuerza Popular party back in 2018 after he refused to support her attempt to impeach sitting president Pedro Pablo Kuczynski. In return, Kenji won Kuczynski’s pardon for their father (although this was promptly reversed by the Supreme Court, postponing his release for six more years). Keiko justified her opposition to Kenji by stating that Fujimori should be fully absolved by the judiciary and not simply exonerated by the executive. Critics pointed out that she was putting the political stakes first, rather than really trying to liberate her ailing father. In 2022, Keiko announced the end of her eighteen-year marriage, though emphasized an amicable separation. This February, Keiko’s own daughter attacked her antiabortion policies to over four hundred thousand followers on Instagram. Keiko attributed the post to healthy political debate and not familial tensions. Keiko’s message of unity is not only a private affair. Peru’s first elected female president has also promised to unite a polarized nation. The past four elections have split votes almost exactly down the middle: each time Keiko has lost, it has been by a tiny margin. Ultimately, she too barely edged the contest, after votes from Peruvian emigrants tipped the balance in her favor. At home, her base is concentrated along the urbanized Pacific coast, coming from industrial cities like Chimbote, Chiclayo, and Trujillo. In the runoff, she captured conservative votes in metropolitan Lima from its flamboyant former mayor, Rafael López Aliaga, a business tycoon and Opus Dei member. Rural districts in the Andes and in the Amazon, meanwhile, lent their backing to leftist Roberto Sánchez. Running for Juntos por el Perú, Sánchez campaigned to redraft the constitution, promoted state-led development and police reform, and promised justice for victims of state repression during the armed struggle of the 1980s and ’90s. More symbolically, Sánchez’s candidacy represented vindication for his ally, Pedro Castillo, who was president for sixteen months before his impeachment in 2022 and who is currently serving eleven years in prison for attempting to close Congress. In the end, Sánchez’s leftist program was trumped by Keiko’s pro-market, strong-state agenda that endorsed hard-line security and the expansion of the army while downplaying the social legacies of the civil conflict. Peru With Order? Unity, in this sense, does not mean true national reconciliation but rather the consolidation of a right-wing populist coalition around the Fujimori surname. Indeed, it is Keiko’s tough stance on crime that has galvanized her supporters, some applauding her father’s violent crusade against Maoist armed group the Shining Path that resulted in their almost total obliteration and put an end to the internal conflict. Whereas in her previous presidential campaigns Keiko had tiptoed away from her father’s legacy, in this attempt she capitalized on his reputation as a strongman. This strategy resonated with residents of informal urban communities in particular. Crime rates in Peru have surged over recent months, becoming a major source of fear. Gang violence has reached unprecedented levels across the country. Low-income neighborhoods are blighted by street theft and extortion. Since 2019, the homicide rate has increased from 7.4 to 10.7 per 100,000 inhabitants. Running under the slogan “Perú con orden” (Peru with Order), Keiko has prioritized public safety and has pledged to dismantle the transnational criminal networks that operate within Peruvian territory. Her security policies state that she will deploy soldiers in high-crime areas, increase prison capacity, reform the penitentiary system, and strengthen the policing of international borders. Championing national defense forces, she also seeks to empower national intelligence agencies, increase the military’s autonomy from the courts, and withdraw from the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. Such authoritarian tendencies suggest that, at least in the war on crime, Keiko’s rule pursues a continuation of Fujimori’s internal politics. Still, Keiko steps into a very different kind of government. In 1990, her father won by a landslide. Two years later, he closed Congress and suspended the constitution before instituting a unicameral constituent assembly designed to condense power in the executive. Keiko has no such mandate. This year marks the restitution of a bicameral chamber after it was dismantled by her father. Fuerza Popular does not have an absolute majority in either the Chamber of Deputies or in the newly established Senate. In order to govern effectively, Keiko will be obliged to form cross-party coalitions. Her legislation will be doubly scrutinized. She will be urged to engage in dialogue by a weary electorate desperate to overcome a decade of hamstrung governance. Peru has seen ten presidents in as many years. Most of these have resigned, have been removed, or have been imprisoned. Some, like late-2010s President Pedro Pablo Kuczynski and then Castillo, have fallen as a result of Keiko’s schemes to utilize congressional powers in pursuit of her own agenda. This weaponization of Congress pays testament to a political system that allows the ambitions of individualistic leaders to congeal in partisan organizations. Yet Keiko is not immune to these machinations either. She has fallen victim once before, jailed for sixteen months when undergoing an investigation for corruption that was later dropped but that might yet reemerge. She will be incentivized, then, to negotiate. Keiko’s broader interpretation of democratic freedom is yet to be seen. On July 28, hundreds of men and women traveled from across the country to the center of Lima to protest her inauguration. Among them were relatives of people killed during the widespread demonstrations against Dina Boluarte, Castillo’s vice president, who came to power with backing from Fuerza Popular after his removal. In the tumultuous months that followed her ascent, Boluarte deployed the military to dissipate protests in southern cities, resulting in the deaths of at least forty-nine civilians. The protesters accuse Keiko of complying with state violence by protecting those responsible for the killings, viewing her election as an indication that Peru endorses a culture of impunity. This pro-Castillo group joins forces with families of those murdered or disappeared by the military death squads that were overseen by Alberto Fujimori in the 1990s. Marching alongside students, socialists, and trade unions, they have resurrected an iconic flag-washing ritual that was used to denounce corruption during the president’s final year in office. In the past, Keiko has largely ignored this popular articulation of the anti-Fujimori movement. This may change, as she too sets out to cleanse Peru.

articles.title: Puerto Rico’s Independence Movement Is Gaining Strength
articles.author: Cruz Bonlarron Martínez
articles.content: In a recent speech in the city of Nashville, former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris spoke about the need to “revisit” several questions about the US political system: the Electoral College, the Supreme Court, and statehood for Puerto Rico and Washington, DC. While the US media was keen to pick up on her comments about the Electoral College and the court, the mention of Puerto Rico was an afterthought. The call for Puerto Rican statehood has become a recurring theme in the mainstream Democratic discourse. However, it owes more to white liberal fantasies of multicultural imperialism than the real desires of the Puerto Rican people for a change in political status. In fact, the Puerto Rican statehood movement is much more aligned with the Republican Party than their Democratic rivals. The country’s current pro-statehood governor, Jenniffer González, is an ardent Republican and Trumpista . If the Democratic consultants who are advising Harris had taken a little time to research contemporary Puerto Rican politics, they would have seen that the independence movement is taking off among the country’s youth. The pro-independence candidate Juan Dalmau made history by winning nearly 31 percent of the votes in the 2024 gubernatorial election. The choice between independence or incorporation into the colonial metropolis has been the defining characteristic of Puerto Rican politics since the nineteenth century. This is a debate that sociologist Rafael Bernabe, a former Puerto Rican senator from the Citizens Victory Movement, traces in Obstinate Star: A History of the Puerto Rico Independence Movement . Bernabe tells the story of the men and women who kept the dream of Puerto Rican independence alive over the past two hundred years, while focusing on the role that the country’s working class played within the movement. An American Nation While often excluded from the conversation about the Latin American independence campaigns of Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín, the Spanish colonies in the insular Caribbean, Cuba, and Puerto Rico provided soldiers to both sides of the conflict. One such soldier whose life Bernabe discusses is Antonio Valero, a Puerto Rican officer in the Spanish army who participated in the Mexican independence negotiations and decided to join the military of the newly independent nation. However, shortly after independence, Valero’s republican ideals put him at odds with Agustín de Iturbide, who had crowned himself Emperor of Mexico, prompting him to flee to Gran Colombia, where he would enlist in the military and fight for Peru’s independence. Valero never stopped dreaming of liberating his homeland and tried to convince Bolívar to free Spain’s remaining Caribbean colonies. This plan almost came to fruition in 1827 but was abandoned due to the possible threats a continuation of the war could pose to Gran Colombia’s newfound independence. In Obstinate Star , Bernabe shows that the dream of Puerto Rican independence did not die with Bolívar’s abandoned invasion of Cuba and Puerto Rico but reconfigured itself as part of a cosmopolitan Antillean identity promoted by a new generation of Cuban and Puerto Rican intellectual patriots. The two leading Puerto Rican figures of this new generation were Ramón Emeterio Betances and Eugenio María de Hostos, both of whom would prove to be key advocates for Puerto Rico’s independence in the late nineteenth century and the intellectual architects of the Puerto Rican nation. Both appear extensively throughout Bernabe’s history: key supporters of the Lares uprising against Spanish colonial rule in 1868, they connected the fight for Puerto Rican independence with the Cuban revolutionary movement and other struggles for liberation in Latin America and Europe. The book also highlights how the independence movement adapted to changing circumstances after the Spanish-American War, when the island became a US colony in 1898, emphasizing the connections and confrontations between sectors of the movement and the growing labor movement on the island. In the 1930s, ’40s, and ’50s, these connections and differences were most pronounced in the eclectic politics of Pedro Albizu Campos and the Puerto Rican Nationalist Party. Albizu Campos espoused a militant populist nationalism that sought to connect Puerto Rico with contemporary social movements in Latin America, bringing together independence supporters of all ideologies, from conservative nationalists to communists. Bernabe is keen to highlight the ideological contradictions within the Nationalist Party and the ways it struggled to win over the working class from the Socialist Party, which supported statehood. Puerto Rico and the US Left Obstinate Star also emphasizes the strong relationship between the Nationalist Party and the US left in this period. The author focuses in particular on the ties linking Albizu Campos to the Communist Party USA and the left-wing New York Congressman Vito Marcantonio. He goes on to analyze the years following the foundation of the Commonwealth in 1952 and shows how the experience of the 1959 Cuban Revolution revived the independence movement. The Pro-Independence Movement (MPI), much like the 26th of July Movement in Cuba, moved toward an open embrace of Marxism-Leninism and eventually transformed into the new Puerto Rican Socialist Party. The Puerto Rican Independence movement went on to follow a similar path to many left-wing forces around the world between the 1960s and the 1980s, becoming increasingly radicalized. During these years, many small armed organizations developed and engaged in actions against US colonialism like the 1981 bombing of Muñiz Air Base and the 1983 Wells Fargo robbery, at the time the largest bank robbery in US history. Bernabe’s account takes care not to romanticize these events while placing them within the broader historical and political conditions in which they took place, intricately breaking down many of the complex debates that unfolded among the Left at that time. During the same period, the Puerto Rican diaspora in the United States sought to identify itself with the island’s independence movement. For some, this meant joining the diaspora section of the Puerto Rican Socialist Party and seeing themselves as part of a divided nation. Bernabe argues that this approach often led to the prioritization of the independence struggle over support for other movements in the US. A contrasting line came from El Comité, an organization that originally emerged from anti-gentrification struggles and advocated for Puerto Ricans in the United States to organize as an oppressed nationality within the multinational US working class rather than as part of a divided nation. The debate between these two positions led to a polarization that continues to exist today between sectors of the Puerto Rican left. On the one hand, there are those who emphasize the need to focus principally on independence; on the other, there are those who seek to organize within the US left while leaving the question of independence for Puerto Ricans still living on the island. This is a debate that the contemporary US left ought to study when trying to engage with the Puerto Rican diaspora. Beyond Tokenization Even though Puerto Rico remains one of the world’s oldest colonies, its independence movement has a rich history that continues today in the electoral success of the Puerto Rican Independence Party and the growing popularity of the independentista pop king Bad Bunny . Bernabe shows that the independence movement is not a monolith but rather a heterogeneous force made up of activists from a wide range of ideologies and backgrounds. Obstinate Star can serve as a key tool for those on the US left who want to understand more about contemporary Puerto Rican politics beyond the success of Bad Bunny and the occasional tokenization of the island by Democratic Party elites. Bernabe also provides a key resource for those on the island and in other Latin American countries looking to understand how, despite the country’s colonial situation, the Puerto Rican independence movement has reflected wider political trends throughout Latin America, from a historian with direct experience in the movement.

articles.title: The End of Oak Street Is Nostalgia Eating Itself
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: The most powerful impact created by The End of Oak Street, a lame nostalgia piece evoking Amblin Entertainment from four decades back, is that this sort of thing really must cease. For a while, Stranger Things managed to pull off a rebooted 1980s Americana entertainment crossed with horror, but now that that’s over at last, it’d be great if we’d all agree to just move on.The classic era of Amblin Entertainment was itself nostalgic for a 1950s Neverland USA. The End of Oak Street is set in 1982, the year of both Steven Spielberg’s E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial and his haunted house film, Poltergeist, and it’s also centered on a white middle-class suburban family experiencing an extraordinary, otherworldly event. The End of Oak Street crosses that scenario with Spielberg’s Jurassic Park (1993), arriving at a plot about an entire suburban neighborhood transported via wormhole to the prehistoric jungle where dinosaurs tromp the earth and feed on everything smaller than they are, which is everything.As in Spielberg’s 1980s films, The End of Oak Street remains absurdly invested in the prosaic woes of a representative nuclear family, no matter what world-shaking events occur. The Spielberg-ish nuclear family is always “troubled” — Mom and Dad are either divorced or on the verge of divorce, and the kids are anxious about that plus their own suburban concerns. Whatever the big event is that will disrupt their lives, dealing with it allows the family to resolve their own personal troubles, and in the end, voilà, everything is all fixed up again, and the representative white middle-class American family is restored to a restabilized world.Just the Pleasantville-like opening shots of The End of Oak Street, featuring idealized middle-class white Americans having a block party on a sunny, pastel-colored day, made me want to bolt out of the theater. They’re actually affluent Americans living in big houses with vast lawns and all the trimmings, but you know they’re supposed to be seen as “middle class,” and the block party gathering is lightly sprinkled with people of color for the sake of plausible deniability.Written and directed by David Robert Mitchell (Under the Silver Lake, It Follows), The End of Oak Street deals with the major and minor travails of the Platt family. They look like they’re living the American dream, but actually their relationships are charged with latent discord. Husband/father Greg (Ewan McGregor) has lost his job and isn’t telling his family why he’s suddenly so eager to deliver pizzas for cash every evening. Wife/mother Denise (Anne Hathaway) spends way too much time in her basement office writing a “novel,” which is actually a lightly disguised autobiography about her unhappy marriage and her desire to flee to New York City to start afresh.Teenage daughter Audrey (Maisy Stella) longs to be an astronomer but says her parents can’t afford to send her to a good school, and younger brother Brian (Christian Convery) roams the neighborhood with his bow-and-arrow set and has an unrequited crush on a local girl who will wind up more interested in Audrey. The family dog, Starbuck, creates all sorts of problems for their irascible neighbor Mel (P. J. Byrne) — barking incessantly all night, for one thing, and running loose in Mel’s yard where he digs. The Platts’ answer to this is to keep Starbuck on a leash when he’s outside but also to leave Starbuck out all night every night, living alone in his doghouse. So naturally, Starbuck continues to bark all night and chews through his leash and runs away just as the likelihood of his being devoured by a dinosaur hits a sudden, unexpected peak.Because suddenly the Platts are in the Mesozoic Era, and their fleeing neighbors are getting eaten by giant reptiles, and the only thing that matters is avoiding becoming dinosaur chow. The single advantage to such a scenario is that it no longer matters that Greg isn’t being honest about why he’s been delivering pizzas or that Denise feels unfulfilled in their marriage or that Starbuck annoys Mel the neighbor — now it’s all a desperate matter of survival.You’d think that, but actually, no. While dodging gigantic chomping apex predators, Greg and Denise are still bickering about their old problems and generally sweating the small stuff. You can take the characters out of white suburbia, but you can’t take the white suburbia out of the characters.If you’re thinking that this is a wild parody of Spielbergian nostalgia movies about these kinds of people and situations, forget it — I had the same hope that faded almost at once. It’s not a funny movie. It’s not an insightful, critically observant movie. It’s barely a movie at all. Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, who can usually be counted on to bring some pizzazz to their roles, phone in a couple of dull performances. The most interesting thing about them in this film is where they’re at as far as plastic surgery and other face-tightening procedures. Their faces are both so smooth now, so free of crow’s feet, puckers, laugh lines, and other pleasing marks of age and experience, that store mannequins look more lifelike and display greater animation.Mitchell directs with a lack of visual flair that’s remarkable considering, you know, dinosaurs and all. Presumably this is supposed to be a goofy summer movie blockbuster, gory and mindlessly amusing, but it was dumped into release in the dog days of August for a reason, and it’s doing mediocre business. In general, critics like it far better than audiences, but why anyone likes it is beyond me.It’s a depressing, zombie-like film, up and moving when it should be long since dead in its grave. May The End of Oak Street be the end of film nostalgia for Steven Spielberg’s film nostalgia.

articles.title: Minnesota Unions Are a Threat to Trump’s Authoritarianism
articles.author: Shane Burley
articles.content: Federal officers had already been arresting Minneapolis activists for months, but the Trump administration’s sweeping indictments of fifteen union members and leaders in June especially turned heads. The charges are centered around 18 U.S.C. § 372: Conspiracy to Impede or Injure a Federal Officer, allegations that could lead to astounding criminal sentences lasting decades. These arrests came as a dozen defendants were fighting for their freedom after attending a demonstration at the Prairieland Detention Center in Alvarado, Texas, near Fort Worth, where one attendee fired on an officer. Vague connections, membership in Signal chats, and, in one case, allegedly moving a box of zines was all the evidence of collusion needed to put some of them away for life. But in Minneapolis, no officer was injured, and none of those facing the stack of federal charges are alleged to have done anything that thousands of others around the Twin Cities, and millions of others around the country, have not done, such as planning for demonstrations, organizing their neighbors using encrypted chat threads, and blockading roads in a desperate effort to slow the deportation machine. The overcharging of these activists is more than just an attempt at chilling resistance and setting a precedent to criminalize the standard course of organizing; its entire logic is based around the notion that these fifteen people presented an unusually pressing threat to the state and its agents. The primary difference between them and tens of thousands of Minnesotans, and millions of those pushing back on Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) around the country, is that all fifteen are union members, many of them union leaders — and given the weight of Minneapolis’s labor movement in the fight against ICE, their organizing was understood as a serious threat to the Trump administration’s attempt to occupy the city. Unions Can Make or Break the Movement Labor unions have been in Donald Trump’s crosshairs from the beginning of his term. From stripping out the bargaining rights of thousands of federal employees to hamstringing the National Labor Relations Board, the federal agency that oversees private sector unions, Trump’s strategy has been to undermine the power of working people to fight back as a prelude to a draconian takeover that splits neighbors apart while sending tens of thousands to prison camps, or worse. One mistake in Trump’s first term is that he did not undercut his opposition from the beginning. He did try to hamper labor, such as with his attempt to disallow automatic dues deduction for employees whose salary was derived from Medicaid/Medicare payments, a move that would have stripped out the financial infrastructure for home care workers. But this effort happened after his opponents had already been prepared to fight, and a joint lawsuit of all West Coast states ultimately halted his progress. When it came to the movement against ICE in Trump’s second term, unions have been particularly visible from the start, such as when Service Employees International Union (SEIU) California State Council and SEIU–United Service Workers West (USWW) President David Huerta was among those arrested early on, responding to the ICE raids that hit Los Angeles during the summer of 2025. Unions like SEIU Local 721 launched rapid-response efforts, many of which were working with groups like the Coalition for Community Self-Defense. And in cities including Minneapolis–St Paul, it became clear that unions were where many workers were organizing to go out into their communities and where they were getting resources to build out their solidarity networks. In Minneapolis, union organizing has also been community organizing. The Minneapolis Federation of Educators ( MFE ) had already been working with a parents’ group, Minneapolis Families for Public Schools, to organize in support of smaller class sizes and good union contracts to stabilize the public school workforce. Those relationships were the seed for what became the network of school patrols that brought thousands of parents to create ICE watch outside the classrooms. Postal workers, seeing that ICE was using post offices as staging grounds, organized to push them out of their worksites. SEIU Local 26 set up routes to drive potentially nervous workers to their jobs so they wouldn’t be exposed to ICE officers by riding public transit. UNITE HERE 17 organized mutual aid networks and got workers involved in direct community support, something that presaged their successful strike only a few weeks later. Both of those unions reported that their membership was hit hard by ICE arrests and was being harassed in the course of doing their work, such as SEIU drivers at the airport. Communications Workers of America (CWA) Local 7250, which organizes telecom workers, approached the ICE occupation as a union issue from the start: their president, Kieran Knutson, was also a founder of the antifascist group Anti-Racist Action in the 1990s. “I think a lot of workers understood. . . . and showed up right away,” says Alec Stewart, one of those who were indicted, a member of the Minneapolis Association of Professional Employees (MAPE). “[Political] divisions kind of melted away, and it became a working-class struggle.” This is part of why he thinks his network was singled out — because it was an example of organized labor using its power to stop ICE. On January 23, these workers joined the 350,000-person general strike , shutting down business as usual across many sectors in Minnesota. All fifteen of those now facing a lengthy trial were active in it, whether through their own union’s projects or through outside groups like Direct Action Minnesota. Trump vs. Minnesota Unions When the Minneapolis indictment first rolled in, unions played an understated but significant role in the language of the indictment itself. The charges highlighted a group called the Black Cat Workers Collective, another union group that attempts to connect radical unionists to talk about direct action organizing both inside and outside the workplace. The indictment splices frightening language about perceived radicalism, recasting commonplace union tactics like “community organizing” and “digital campaigning” as pieces of a violent conspiracy and “working class” identity as suspicious. The general strike’s infrastructure sits at the center of the indictment’s claim. The strike required groups to help people commute to the city center or to blockade roads — all alleged criminal behavior the government is charging defendants with, thus extending the veil of a criminal conspiracy to the entire labor movement that rallied together. The indictment says defendants “infiltrated and exploited lawful protests,” part of the outside-agitator narrative crucial to Trump’s reframing of anti-deportation protesters as “antifa.” Community organizing and building “strength through numbers” are labeled a piece of the criminal conspiracy, which casts civic engagement and public protest as illegal and again creates a rhetorical bridge between union organizing and “antifa.” Worker assemblies were likewise mentioned, as was the potential that these organizations, and those charged, could be working toward another general strike against ICE’s impunity. The defense team for Isaac Sant, an SEIU member and one of those arrested, recently filed a motion related to discovery that ultimately revealed programs from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) to surveil organizations across Minneapolis–St Paul. In what they labeled Operation Puppet Master and Operation Whipple, HSI ran an undercover investigation of MFE, MAPE, SEIU Local 26, and the statewide AFL-CIO federation. HSI investigated SEIU’s finances in secret, looking to see if they were involved in “domestic terrorist financing,” which they did by going to the union local’s US Bank chapter as well as compelling the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to search through various SEIU transactions. CWA’s PAC expenditures were audited, including those that ostensibly were made during Trump’s second election campaign. The investigation even swept a Canadian union local into the mix. These inquiries were not relegated just to union locals from the Minneapolis area with some direct connection to the protests but to the national unions representing, in some cases, millions of workers coast-to-coast. The documents reveal that HSI placed undercover agents at union halls as well as other places like churches and schools and union-heavy demonstrations including No Kings. At one January 19 meeting at a taqueria, they listened along to “a general discussion on the upcoming walk out on ICE event being held on January 23.” According to the government, MFE Local 59 is especially significant in this conspiracy, given that some members self-organized outside of their union roles. (The name “Operation Puppet Master” fits with the administration’s conspiratorial view of protest movements, suggesting there must be covert interests pulling the strings behind the scenes, rather than simply an organic response to tens of thousands of armed federal officers dragging families from their homes.) The investigation did not begin after an alleged blockade or assault plot had been identified, or any identifiable illegal action had taken place. It was instead a chance to monitor the regional labor movement and plan an indictment pattern that could go after union leaders and influential community members. “I think we have a strong history of very well connected and active unions in this state. . . . So no, I’m not surprised that this attack on the working class was also an attack on that union strength,” says Stewart. The defense team’s motion for discovery reads: It concluded, with no evidence (but obvious political animus), that numerous Twin Cities unions and non-profit organizations were involved in a widespread conspiracy to violate 18 U.S.C. § 111 . . . and it surveilled and surreptitiously gathered financial records generated by these organizations despite the lack of any connection between those organizations and criminal conduct,” reads the defense team’s motion for discovery. Labor Needs to Flex Its Muscle The defendants are fighting the charges and have received vocal support from the rest of the labor movement. Because of the Trump administration’s ongoing assault on unions and, in particular, on public sector workers and essential services, there has been a shift in the culture of organized labor broadly. The Federal Unionist Network (FUN) grew out of the historic weakness of federal worker unions. When Elon Musk and his Department of Government Efficiency slashed public services and Trump attacked federal worker unions, FUN organized to defend both their jobs and the people who depend on the work they do. When Trump punished universities for their students’ pro-Palestine activism, deported students, and sought to crack down on professors’ academic freedom, the American Association of University Professors fought to defend education. The national American Federation of Teachers, of which MFE Local 59 is an affiliate, offered mass action and street medic trainings to provide skills necessary to support protests where ICE may injure community members. While unions are an essential piece of this fight, they can also be slow moving, which is why rank-and-file members have been collaborating across unions to move their organizations to take a more publicly militant stand. Left-labor coalitions like Jobs With Justice, Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) labor working groups, and networks building out of Labor Notes trainings have provided intermediate connections that members can coordinate in to move their federations and executive boards to action in support of political prisoners and against ICE’s deportations. While some labor leaders have hoped silence on divisive issues will allow them to escape the worst of Trump’s attacks, it is unions’ very existence that presents the greatest threat to the administration’s agenda. The labor movement’s decline over the past forty years is due largely to its inaction — and the movement only has a future if it can show that solidarity is the antidote to authoritarian repression.

articles.title: What Multilateralism Looks Like After US Decline
articles.author: Juliano Fiori
articles.content: Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva responded with justified defiance to recent confirmation that the United States government would impose a 25 percent tariff on Brazilian exports. Among the “acts, policies, and practices” that the Office of the United States Trade Representative deemed “unreasonable or discriminatory” and worthy of formal investigation, it cited Brazilian electronic payment services. The Trump administration has frequently denounced Pix, an instant payment mechanism maintained by Brazilian banks without intermediation by US firms such as Visa and Mastercard. However, the imposition of these tariffs is also one of a growing number of measures aimed at undermining Lula’s government ahead of elections in October, as the United States seeks privileged access to Brazil’s abundant source of rare earth elements. A spokesperson for the Brazilian president questioned the legitimacy of the investigation, stating that it was “not based on multilateral trade rules.” But there is a bigger problem. While national governments still invoke such rules in defense of their sovereignty, the conditions that enabled the expansion of multilateralism in the twentieth century no longer exist. Though the Trump administration’s brazen disregard of international norms and institutions might intuitively be identified as evidence of this, it is not the most important indicator: after all, it is the prerogative of hegemonic power to circumvent universal rules while policing others’ adherence to them. Of more consequence is the United States’ apparent inability to reshape these rules in accordance with its own evolving geostrategy. And as Washington has eschewed multilateralism, its global preeminence in the exercise of coercion has also waned. Given the effective absence of the United States from existing multilateral institutions, attempts to give them new meaning – not least by revisionist states such as China and Russia – have been used to undermine American hegemony itself. But as Donald Trump paints the world with new targets, adversaries of circumstance as well as systemic rivals are also responding in kind. Economic Warfare Particularly indicative, in this regard, are changes in the conduct of economic warfare. The US dollar has been the global currency of reference since the Bretton Woods Agreement of 1944, allowing Washington unique control over international flows of capital and commodities. Through the imposition of distinct forms of “blockade,” from sanctions to tariffs to maritime sieges, the United States has conditioned economic relations in a manner that, for a time, served to produce a system of consent to its imperial power. However, such measures have forced actions that have ultimately contributed to the erosion of its global hegemony. Under the strain of American sanctions, for example, Russia, Iran, and Venezuela have pursued de-dollarization strategies, settling trade in other currencies, yuan in particular. Yet as noted recently by historian Nicholas Mulder, many states have responded to growing coercion from Washington by developing “not just evasion routes but economic counter-weapons of their own.” The threat of reciprocal tariffs has been the most common recourse among states targeted by the second Trump administration’s economic coercion. The most dramatic consequence of this approach was the de facto mutual trade embargo maintained between the United States and China for a month in mid-2025, after Chinese President Xi Jinping repeatedly matched Trump in escalating tariffs. In response to the recent announcement of tariffs on Brazilian exports, Lula’s spokesperson invoked Brazil’s Economic Reciprocity Law, which permits the government to respond proportionately to measures by other states that undermine its competitiveness. But he nonetheless reaffirmed the government’s commitment to multilateralism by promising to pursue redress through the World Trade Organization’s dispute-settlement mechanism. But if trade protections have regained international legitimacy as a means of defending national sovereignty, the use of physical barriers to trade as an economic “counter-weapon” has threatened more immediate and generalized consequences. For decades, energy-security analysts and foreign-policy strategists had studied the possibility that Iran might effectively block the Strait of Hormuz. The materialization of this possibility, and the introduction by Iran of a toll on the passage of ships through the strait, should have been less surprising than Trump’s short-lived determination to do the same. However, Iran’s defensive actions, in response to the war launched upon it by the United States and Israel, are far more remarkable for their systemic implications. In his acclaimed account of the Great Depression, historian Charles Kindleberger contended that the stability of the world economy depended upon the existence of a single hegemonic state able to lead through the provision of international public goods. By 1973, when The World in Depression was published, the United States had long since consolidated its global hegemony, touting its protection for freedom of the seas as one such public good even as it exercised its hegemonic prerogative to control the flow of trade through international waterways. If Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz and its request for Houthi allies to close the Bab al-Mandeb Strait pose a direct challenge to freedom of the seas, the failure of the United States to ensure adherence to this principle is a further indication of the collapse of its hegemony. In a world after the hegemonic order of the United States, multilateral institutions, not least those of the United Nations, are losing political currency. They are becoming less effective in imposing constraints on national interests. These institutions in general were enabled and sustained within the system of consent of American hegemony. Though they will continue to serve as sites of defensive appeal against imperial impositions and hypocrisy, great-power dominance is likely to engender more direct, coercive responses. However, for middle powers in particular, multilateralism provides opportunity for their own relative influence to be exercised in the construction of collective endeavors that better protect their interests. Indeed, middle powers were instrumental in the definition of many UN institutions. Middle Powers In his speech to the World Economic Forum this January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called upon middle powers to “build a new order that encompasses our values, such as respect for human rights, sustainable development, solidarity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of the various states.” But for all his moral posturing, it was recognition of his country’s limited sway, and thus its interest in combining forces with others in a similar position, that stimulated Carney to assume leadership in the promotion of middle-power coalitions. Indeed, he made it clear that upholding these values was not of primary concern a couple of months later, when he announced his support for the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran. Without the consolidation of a new global hegemonic order, new modes of multilateral engagement will emerge. Regional and bloc formations, already on the rise in the first quarter of the twenty-first century, are likely to play a more prominent role. But, so far, the global import of middle-power initiatives has been limited. The current US government seems keen to contain their influence. In mid-July, the United States Under Secretary of War for Policy, Elbridge Colby, posted a thread on X about collective strategy among middle powers, in which he argued that it was based on “a faulty understanding of international relations.” “‘Middle powers’ don’t have a coherent basis for alignment,” he added. However, the strategic convergence of middle powers will not be determined primarily by the ideological inclinations of their governments. Rather, middle powers will be compelled to cultivate diplomatic innovations — even when coalition-building is not viable or preferable — as a consequence of their position in relation to imperial powers. Lula’s positioning of Brazil as an international mediator is indicative. Consonant with Brazil’s own foreign-policy tradition, its role, alongside Turkey, in previous negotiations regarding Iran’s nuclear program demonstrated a willingness to perform this systemic function amid earlier signs of relative American decline. Lula’s offers to mediate peace talks between Ukraine and Russia, and between Venezuela and the United States, serve as more recent examples. And yet, such diplomacy will not provide immediate defense against the coercion of the Trump administration. Economic countermeasures, playing on China’s rivalry to the United States, will then also become increasingly central to Brazilian efforts to assert national sovereignty. The end of order does not necessarily imply the end of multilateralism. The major structural transformations of our time will produce new channels for international cooperation, based on shared interests. The extent to which these channels of cooperation might constrain great-power dominance will depend on the middle powers’ subsequent investment in expanding them.

articles.title: Realism or Resisting Immersion?
articles.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
articles.content: There’s an old Marxist-Leninist tweet from a gadfly who went by the name of Phil Greaves: “ Star Wars is fascist, Harry Potter is fascist neo-feudal dreck, selfie-obsession is fascist, British soap operas are fascist, sci-fi is generally fascist, ironic detachment is fascist, porn is fascist. Masscult under imperialism is inherently fascistic. Sorry to spoil your ‘fun’.” And the mad lad who has since protected his tweets replied to himself soon after: “One day people will ask: ‘How did Anglo-Americans not see their own fascism?’ And part of the answer will be: ‘Because they were entertained by it.’” The point Greaves is getting at is how the current moment attempts to overwhelm you as an individual with spectacle at all times, and to hypnotize you in a way. It is easier for the state to alienate you and keep you locked into regular consumer behavior if you are watching ambivalently, without thinking, allowing yourself to be immersed in something whether it be the new Avatar film, alcohol or drug abuse, or porn addiction. Think about how the so-called algorithm induces schizophrenia in you as a subject. You first see a selfie from your friend back home for the holidays, and next, you see an ad for a political candidate paid by a subsidiary of AIPAC. Then you see from the news account of your choice Palestinian bodies mutilated by either our government’s or Israel’s. Then you see a meme that you have to Google in order to understand. In mere seconds, you have hopped around the world, and your attention has shifted again, again, and again. The problem here is one of immersion. These media objects, whether we talk about the Marvel Cinematic Universe or virtually-augmented point-of-view porn, like cigarettes, come in regular enough doses to give you your fix, and yet something feels missing. Mark Fisher calls this condition “depressive hedonia.” Here’s Fisher in chapter 4 of Capitalist Realism : “Many of the teenage students I encountered seemed to be in a state of what I would call depressive hedonia. Depression is usually characterized as a state of anhedonia, but the condition I’m referring to is constituted not by an inability to get pleasure so much as an inability to do anything else except pursue pleasure. There is a sense that ‘something is missing’ – but no appreciation that this mysterious, missing enjoyment can only be accessed beyond the pleasure principle. In large part this is a consequence of students’ ambiguous structural position, stranded between their old role as subjects of disciplinary institutions and their new status as consumers of services. In his crucial essay ‘Postscript on Societies of Control’, Deleuze distinguishes between the disciplinary societies described by Foucault, which were organized around the enclosed spaces of the factory, the school and the prison, and the new control societies, in which all institutions are embedded in a dispersed corporation. ” Regarding that last line, in the new MCU film, Spider-Man: Brand New Day , Zendaya’s character gets offered a good job, but she turns it down because it’s for an evil corporation. Her friend asks if all corporations are evil. She says “Yes.” In the context of the film, this is one of the things Peter Parker loves about her: her ethical moral compass. But in the reality the film exists in, this line is ironic by being a product of Disney, whose name is interestingly missing from both the front and end credits. Zendaya’s character’s refusing to work for a corporation is proven to be hypocritical, as the actress has chosen for the better part of a decade to work almost exclusively for them. And yet, when she kisses Tom Holland, her real-life boyfriend, the audience applauded nonetheless. The Soviet film theorist Lev Kuleshov wrote in his landmark piece of film theory “The Principles of Montage”: “The artist’s relationship to his surrounding reality, his view of the world, is not merely expressed in the entire process of shooting, but in the montage as well, in the capacity to see and to present the world around him. A variety of social encounters, a class struggle takes place in reality, and the artist’s existence within a particular social class influences his world-view. Artists with differing world-views each perceive the reality surrounding them differently; they see events differently, discuss them differently, show them, imagine them, and join them to another differently. Thus, film montage, as the entire work of filmmaking, is inextricably linked to the artist’s world-view and his ideological purpose.” If we take this as true and look at the dominant mode of filmmaking in America and the West in the past 50 years since the end of New Hollywood with the release of Jaws and Star Wars (pick your poison), it’s obvious that the dominant mode of filmmaking has been immersion. When James Cameron’s Avatar was released and pushed forward the trend of 3D and fully digital spaces, the main point of praise was how ‘immersive’ it was. With Avatar: The Way of the Water , this was taken forward with new, technically difficult footage never before possible, both with underwater 3D footage requiring technological advancement allowing each piece of the human face to be recorded in a liquid environment where facial features are distorted. Some left-wing filmmakers, like the undersung Paul W.S. Anderson, have attempted to work from within the system, creating movies with revolutionary politics like Resident Evil: Retribution , which features images like that of a private military group falling beneath the superstructure of an old Soviet base, being crushed by the very simulacra they used to poison the world. But Anderson, too, like Cameron, was victim to the desire to immerse the audience and give us our dopamine fixes. He even used technology from the state to lull audiences into a kind of stupor, turning shots meant to recall to the viewer the torture at the hands of the fascists in Salò, or 120 Days of Sodom into images meant to entertain the viewer. He used NASA cameras shooting upwards of 10,000 frames per second for very beautiful slow motion photography. There’s surely a joke to be made from the old Maoist Jean-Luc Godard’s line about cinema being the truth at 24 frames per second, updated to 10,000 lies per second through social-democrat Paul W.S. Anderson’s cinema. There’s a bizarre video that came out in 2012 featuring Marxist filmmaker Michael Haneke and CIA plant John Krasinski in the Hollywood Reporter where Haneke explains how Spielberg’s Schindler’s List is an incredibly manipulative film because of how it turns the Holocaust into entertainment. We, the audience, begin to fear whether the characters will be gassed or not. The gas of Auschwitz is turned from a real historical object into a literary device, another example of Chekov’s gun. Haneke’s films, by contrast, are cold and impersonal. His first theatrical feature, The Seventh Continent , spends ten minutes following a family getting out of bed. We don’t see their faces, instead their feet as they tie their shoes and their hands as they eat. This is a Brechtian approach to filmmaking, meaning Haneke is using the distancing effect. He wants the audience to be at a remove from what he is presenting, and instead the audience thinks about it instead of being immersed in whatever world is being shown. His films echo the words of the great Soviet filmmaker and film theorist Sergei Eisenstein, who wrote in “A Dialectical Approach to Film Form”: “Step by step, by a process of comparing each new image with the common denotation, power is accumulated behind a process that can be formally identified with that of logical deduction. The decision to release these ideas, as well as the method used, is already intellectually conceived. The conventional descriptive form for film leads to the formal possibility of a kind of filmic reasoning. While the conventional film directs the emotions, this suggests an opportunity to encourage and direct the whole thought process as well.” This is a mode of filmmaking that rejects emotional manipulation alone and instead wants the audience to deduce the logic of the material reality being presented. When you go to the movies, you interact with filmed reality. It’s ultimately a kind of materialistic art, when you look towards its essence. But in America, from the big studios down to micro-budget filmmakers here in Chicago, there is a push towards immersion. We filmmakers are entertained by the studios, and so we aspire to work for the studios, just as naïvely as the working man believes that one day he, too, will be a billionaire. Audience members broke box office records recently watching the new, fascist Spider-Man movie. What’s troubling is that there aren’t many alternatives. I Want Your Sex , from Queer New Wave icon Gregg Araki, demands an attention to the roles shown and the characters’ class relations, but its obvious ideology attacking hedonism appears to have been lost on the critical masses who praise it for its explicit sex scenes in a puritanical era. Yet the sex scenes and the context of the characters show that the puritanical approach is more ‘correct’ than the perspective espoused by Olivia Wilde, even though her words appear alluring. She roofies Cooper Hoffman’s character, explicitly grooms him, and abuses him. Somehow this is lost on many viewers. When talking about contemporary socialist films, not a whole lot of names pop up here in the Americas. Boots Riley comes to mind immediately, but the question quickly arises if his filmmaking is even particularly socialist. His individual opinions are, yes, but the form of it all? Even if his characters in I Love Boosters end up cheering a general strike, the form of his film still relies on immersion. The film form is still capitalistic to the core, from its production model to how the movie moves from shot to shot, even if its main plot device is a dialectical materialism device. This just appropriates left wing language for the sake of corporate profit. So then, what is to be desired? We must, as filmmakers, keep the audience at a remove from the world of the film, and we as viewers must leave the film world that we watch at a distance and reject any parasocial emotions that fill inside of us. We must desire to be challenged formally and accept that we might be bored from time to time. Sometimes, we might even desire to be bored. Later in chapter 4 of Capitalist Realism , Mark Fisher says: “Ask students to read for more than a couple of sentences and many – and these are A-level students mind you – will protest that they can’t do it. The most frequent complaint teachers hear is that it’s boring. It is not so much the content of the written material that is at issue here; it is the act of reading itself that is deemed to be ‘boring’. What we are facing here is not just time-honored teenage torpor, but the mismatch between a postliterate ‘New Flesh’ that is ‘too wired to concentrate’ and the conning, concentrational logics of decaying disciplinary systems. To be bored simply means to be removed from the communicative sensation-stimulus matrix of texting, YouTube and fast food; to be denied, for a moment, the constant flow of sugary gratification on demand. Some students want Nietzsche in the same way that they want a hamburger; they fail to grasp – and the logic of the consumer system encourages this misapprehension – that the indigestibility, the difficulty is Nietzsche.” We must deny immediate satisfaction to contemplate ideas, to depict ideas, and to challenge the viewer to try to understand them. In Angela Schalenec’s Passing Summer , a writer goes up to a publisher who is disappointed at her reliance upon elliptical sentences. He says something like, ‘at some point, I just wanted to read a normal novel. Do you not want to be understood?’ And she says, “I want to be understood.” And yet Schalenec, in each of the films she has made since that 2002 film, has not removed her own elliptical, naturalistic, and difficult narrative decisions. She wants to be understood, but she doesn’t want to do so by leaving her principles at the wayside. And so, neither must we, as socialists. The post Realism or Resisting Immersion? appeared first on Midwest Socialist .

articles.title: On Ecuador: When the Referees Join a Team
articles.author: DSA National Statements
articles.content: A statement of the Democratic Socialists of America International Committee, July 2026. En español a continuación. What is happening in Ecuador is a coup conducted without tanks. Its weapons are electoral councils, tribunals, and prosecutors, and its result is the one every coup seeks: a government that no longer has to face its opponents on equal terms. In a single week of July, the government of President Daniel Noboa closed three of the channels through which Ecuadorians contest power, each time by a lawful-looking decision of an ostensibly neutral body. On July 15, the National Electoral Council refused to release the forms citizens need to gather signatures for a recall of the president, a right written into the constitution, ending the effort before anyone could sign. 1 Days earlier the Constitutional Court had refused even to hear the appeal of the Citizen Revolution, the largest opposition force, against its own suspension, citing a rule that blocks review during an election period, which is the only period when the suspension bites. 2 Then the electoral tribunal suspended AMIGO, the movement under which Citizen Revolution candidates had arranged to run, one day before the deadline to register alliances. 3 Throughout, Noboa litigated against the recall aimed at him before the very council deciding whether it could proceed. 4 This is not a seizure of power in the night. It is the steady conversion of the referees, the electoral council, the courts, the prosecutor, into instruments of the incumbent. Each step survives inspection on its own. Together they let a president choose his opponents. It did not begin with paperwork. During last autumn’s national strike against austerity, security forces killed three protesters and charged demonstrators as terrorists. 5 And it is not only Ecuador’s affair. Ecuadorians voted in November 2025 to reject foreign military bases; the United States deployed personnel to Manta anyway, and by July the chief of U.S. Southern Command was in Quito reviewing Noboa’s security plan in person. 6 Our own government has set aside a vote of the Ecuadorian people, which places a particular duty on socialists in the U.S. To the citizens’ platform Revoca EC and the attorney Washington Andrade; to Leonidas Iza, acting as president of Ecuarunari; to the peasant, labor, and teachers’ organizations, FENOCIN, the FUT, the Frente Popular, and the UNE, who filed the second recall petition against austerity and the agreement with the International Monetary Fund; and to every rank-and-file member of the Citizen Revolution whose party the electoral tribunal has barred from the ballot: we see you, and we stand with you. We do not write to instruct anyone in Ecuador how to conduct their struggle. We write to affirm a principle that stands above any single party’s fortunes: the recall belongs to the people, not to a party, and the right to appear on a ballot cannot depend on the incumbent’s convenience. The government suspended its largest opposition without ever proving the charge, because it timed the suspension to the one period when the courts are barred from reviewing it. A case that cannot survive review is not a case. It is a tactic. DSA members: raise Ecuador where you are. Bring this statement to your chapter, and demand that your own representatives end the U.S. military and police cooperation that underwrites this repression. The local elections of November 29 will test whether Ecuador’s doors are narrowed or shut. Doors closed by law can be reopened by law, but only while some remain open, and solidarity is one of the things that keeps them open. The recall is not a party’s weapon. It is the people’s. From Quito to Chicago, our struggle is one. El Universo , July 15, 2026. Primicias , July 15, 2026. La República , July 17, 2026. Qué Noticias , July 8, 2026. El Universo , October 23, 2025. International IDEA , November 2025; La Jornada , July 18, 2026. Sobre el Ecuador: cuando los árbitros se suman a un equipo Declaración del Comité Internacional de los Socialistas Democráticos de América (DSA), julio de 2026. Lo que ocurre en el Ecuador es un golpe sin tanques. Sus armas son los consejos electorales, los tribunales y la Fiscalía, y su resultado es el que persigue todo golpe: un gobierno que ya no tiene que enfrentarse a sus adversarios en igualdad de condiciones. En una sola semana de julio, el gobierno del presidente Daniel Noboa cerró tres de los canales por los que los ecuatorianos disputan el poder, cada vez mediante la decisión, en apariencia lícita, de un organismo supuestamente neutral. El 15 de julio, el Consejo Nacional Electoral se negó a entregar los formularios que la ciudadanía necesita para recolectar firmas por la revocatoria del mandato del presidente, un derecho inscrito en la Constitución, poniendo fin al proceso antes de que alguien pudiera firmar. Días antes, la Corte Constitucional se había negado incluso a conocer el recurso de la Revolución Ciudadana, la mayor fuerza de oposición, contra su propia suspensión, invocando una norma que impide la revisión durante el período electoral, el único período en que la suspensión le duele. Luego el Tribunal Contencioso Electoral suspendió a AMIGO, el movimiento bajo el cual habían acordado inscribirse las candidaturas de la Revolución Ciudadana, un día antes del plazo para inscribir alianzas. Durante todo el proceso, Noboa litigó contra la revocatoria dirigida a él ante el mismo consejo que decidía si podía avanzar. No es la toma del poder en la noche. Es la conversión paulatina de los árbitros, el consejo electoral, las cortes, la Fiscalía, en instrumentos del oficialismo. Cada paso resiste el escrutinio por separado. Juntos, permiten que un presidente escoja a sus adversarios. No empezó con el papeleo. Durante el paro nacional del año pasado contra el ajuste, las fuerzas de seguridad mataron a tres manifestantes y procesaron a manifestantes por terrorismo. Y no es solo un asunto del Ecuador. Los ecuatorianos votaron en noviembre de 2025 en contra de las bases militares extranjeras; Estados Unidos desplegó igual a su personal en Manta y, para julio, el jefe del Comando Sur estaba en Quito revisando en persona el plan de seguridad de Noboa. Nuestro propio gobierno ha desconocido una votación del pueblo ecuatoriano, lo que impone un deber particular a las y los socialistas de este país. A la plataforma ciudadana Revoca EC y al abogado Washington Andrade; a Leonidas Iza, en su calidad de presidente de la Ecuarunari; a las organizaciones campesinas, sindicales y docentes, la FENOCIN, el FUT, el Frente Popular y la UNE, que presentaron la segunda solicitud de revocatoria contra el ajuste y el acuerdo con el Fondo Monetario Internacional; y a cada militante de base de la Revolución Ciudadana cuyo movimiento el Tribunal Contencioso Electoral ha excluido de la papeleta: les vemos y estamos con ustedes. No escribimos para indicarle a nadie en el Ecuador cómo conducir su lucha. Escribimos para afirmar un principio que está por encima de la suerte de cualquier partido: la revocatoria pertenece al pueblo, no a un partido, y el derecho a aparecer en la papeleta no puede depender de la conveniencia del oficialismo. Un gobierno que suspende a su principal oposición en la única ventana en la que las cortes no mirarán no ha ganado una discusión. Se ha negado a tenerla. A las y los afiliados de DSA: levanten el tema del Ecuador donde estén. Lleven esta declaración a su sección, inviten a estas organizaciones a hablar directamente con nosotros y exijan a sus propios representantes que pongan fin a la cooperación militar y policial estadounidense que sostiene esta represión. Las elecciones seccionales del 29 de noviembre pondrán a prueba si las puertas del Ecuador se quedan estrechadas o cerradas. Las puertas cerradas por la ley pueden reabrirse por la ley, pero solo mientras algunas sigan abiertas, y la solidaridad es una de las cosas que las mantiene abiertas. La revocatoria no es el arma de un partido. Es la del pueblo. De Quito a Chicago, nuestra lucha es una sola.
