articles.title: De la Espriella ends Colombia’s peace policy, opens door to US military operations
articles.author: BreakThrough News
articles.content: In his first week in office, despite fumbling the response to the devastating earthquake, Abelardo De la Espriella made good on his promise to end the state policy of promoting peace and launch military actions against armed groups in the country. Beginning on August 9, the Armed Forces launched an offensive in which, according to the Army, four members of the FARC dissident group were killed in Meta, and two others from the Clan del Golfo were killed in Antioquia. Between August 10 and 11, in Catatumbo, authorities reported the deaths of two ELN members, as well as the destruction of two bunkers and five camps. In addition, the government celebrated the death of Dubán Ramiro Castillo, identified as the leader of the Mordisco dissident group, in an attack by military forces in Valle del Cauca on August 12. The response from dissident groups was swift. Using drones and other methods, these irregular groups have launched counterattacks. On August 12 in Huila, one officer was reported killed and several soldiers wounded. Another attack in Cauca left several service members wounded. However, the most significant attack occurred on August 14, in which a sergeant was killed and four soldiers were wounded when they were attacked by drones in El Carmen, Catatumbo. This attack comes on top of another carried out in the days prior in Northern Santander, where the Army stated that 43 drones carrying explosives were used against a military base. Likewise, human rights organizations reported that military operations had caused serious injuries to three farmers in the Catatumbo region, as well as damage to homes and the displacement of people toward the El Tarra area. The government, for its part, stated that it has not deliberately harmed civilians. Thus, Colombia appears to be gradually returning to the days of all-out war. De la Espriella has already warned that the offensive will be carried out forcefully until total submission is achieved, and that there will be no room for dialogue. This approach is not new in Colombia. In fact it was employed extensively by the administration of far-right former president Álvaro Uribe Vélez and it not only failed to end the violence in Colombia, but intensified it and affected, in particular, the civilian population of the rural areas where the conflict is primarily taking place. Now once, again, in many regions of the country that have consistently ratified the need for peace at the ballot box and in the streets, this peace seems to be slipping through their fingers. Abelardo’s promise to end peace One of the most persistent arguments of the then-Colombian presidential candidate Abelardo de la Espriella was the suspension and dismantling of the state’s peace-promotion policy. The initiative, launched by the right-wing government of Juan Manuel Santos, aimed to de-escalate violence in a country that has been embroiled in armed conflict for several decades. Santos succeeded in signing a peace agreement in 2016 in Havana, Cuba, with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the country’s largest insurgent group. The former president also made significant progress in talks with the National Liberation Army (ELN), which opened up a potential path toward an end to the violence. True avenues towards peace had been largely blocked until then. Santos was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2016, the same year the Havana Accords were ratified. A large portion of the Colombian right wing (especially its most radical faction) opposed the peace agreement. This faction has historically advocated for total war against insurgent groups – that is, until they are completely subdued by force. In a country as vast as Colombia, with so many internal contradictions, however, no government has ever achieved this goal, despite grandiloquent declarations of war and victory. De la Espriella has now once again embodied this rhetoric , which seeks to make constant internal conflict a way of life for society. There have been many arguments regarding the drive to normalize violence, ranging from the economic benefits that various Colombian and foreign groups derive from fomenting war, to the desire to keep the left off the electoral stage and constantly associate it with armed factions. A new US-backed military offensive Whatever the case may be, De la Espriella has decided to continue a radical right-wing political tradition and declare an end to the state’s “Peace” policy, in favor of resuming widespread military operations against irregular armed groups. To this end, he has once again, as tradition dictates, turned to Washington, which, according to its Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, would launch military operations “on the ground” in Colombia and other countries in the region. If we add to this the nearly $1 billion that the Trump administration disbursed to the recently inaugurated Colombian president, we gain a clearer picture of the course that the close alliance between Bogotá and Washington will take – an alliance that has been one of the most valued and carefully nurtured relationships in US history. Yet we should also not discount that the previous government, led by the progressive Gustavo Petro, did not carry out any military operations against insurgent groups. The Colombian Army has not ceased its fight against these groups since they first emerged. But it is true that certain truces and ceasefires had been established until several splinter groups of the former FARC and ELN resumed armed operations in response to what they considered a breach of the agreements. Between August 7 and 8 alone, the first 48 hours of his mandate, six incidents carried out by FARC dissidents and other groups were reported in areas such as San Roque, Tolima, Cauca, etc. Thus, De la Espriella inherits a country embroiled in armed conflict. But, as he has stated, De la Espriella, like other right-wing Colombian leaders, hopes to shift the strategy from containment and dialogue to an all-out offensive. With support from an even more aggressive US administration, the result could be devastating for the people of Colombia.

articles.title: Right-Hand Man or Biggest Mistake? Åsmund Egge’s Grigory Zinoviev
articles.author: Panagiotis Sotiris
articles.content: Åsmund Egge. Grigory Zinoviev: Lenin’s Right-hand Man . Routledge Histories of Central and Eastern Europe. London and New York: Routledge of Taylor & Francis, 2026. Pp. xi, 368. Reviewed by Clayton Black At roughly ten years of age (no precise dates are available), Ovsei-Gershen Aronovich Radomyshelsky, who later identified himself as Ovsei Radomyslsky, Grigory Radomyslsky, a variety of noms de plume , and eventually Grigory Zinoviev, reportedly pushed a friend into ‘a pit for leaching unslaked lime’ (p. 12). The burns to Ovsei-Gershen’s friend eventually killed him, an incident that Åsmund Egge (and his source, Vyacheslav Samokhodkin) speculates so traumatised the young Zinoviev that it may have caused him to attempt suicide. The tragedy may also explain the oft-documented emotional outbursts and fits of panic once Zinoviev rose to the pinnacle of power in the Bolshevik revolution. Zinoviev’s childhood tragedy may or may not have left lifelong scars on his personality and behaviour. Egge stops short of a thoroughgoing psychological analysis. He must nevertheless confront an array of well-established characterisations of Zinoviev that dominate the published record. Indeed, nearly every attempt to reckon with Zinoviev—including my own—spills much ink recounting the man’s physical attributes (pudgy, wild hair, pale, high “tenor” voice, weak constitution), personal failings (moodiness, vainglory, womanising), theoretical shallowness, and infamous moments of indecision or cowardice in the revolution and first years of Soviet power. Zinoviev presents such an unappealing figure to most historians that few have ventured beyond superficial mentions of him. One colleague of mine who works on related subjects once repeatedly used the word “odious” to describe him. Such appraisals may help explain why, until recently, no full-length biography of the man had been written, and articles and dissertations that focus on him sound almost apologetic in their introductions. Yet not until his conclusion does Egge pose four critical questions: How could such a deeply unsympathetic and inept person manage to build up a significant following – the so-called Zinovievists? How could a person “with no understanding of political power and no ability to treat people”, to quote E. H. Carr . . . manage to build such a unified and powerful organisation as the one Zinoviev established in Leningrad? How is it possible that Zinoviev was considered by many to be Lenin’s successor if he was so inept and unpleasant in every way? And how could the other leaders of the party accept that such mediocrity could occupy the most senior positions in the party? (p. 342) Egge’s subtitle hints unintentionally at one possible answer to these questions, one that reflects the sentiment of Victor Serge, who called Zinoviev ‘Lenin’s biggest mistake’. [1] Though ‘right-hand man’ (depending on the reader’s view of Lenin) might suggest a favourable orientation to its subject, it may also imply what the historiography has tended to assume: Lenin placed his trust in Zinoviev, a trust that was ill-deserved and that Zinoviev was unable to parlay into successful leadership after the leader’s death in 1924. It is thus not difficult to understand historians’ reluctance to study the man: they see him merely as a mouthpiece for Lenin with few original ideas or contributions to the revolution; he was not as sympathetic as Nikolai Bukharin and offered no clearly articulated ‘alternative’ to what Joseph Stalin was creating; and, while Leon Trotsky may have identified Stalin also as a ‘mediocrity’ in the Party, neither Stalin nor his subsequent career require explanation for the attention they receive from historians. Egge’s book is not an apology for Zinoviev. It is, rather, an attempt to offer a dispassionate account of a man who, for too long, received far less attention than his record at the apex of Bolshevik power would seem to warrant. Yuri Zhukov’s 2021 monograph, though it was the first full-length biography, used Zinoviev’s story as a part of a larger argument celebrating the Stalinist rejection of world revolution. [2] Recent dissertations by V.M. Vikhrov, V.N. Samokhodkin, A.Yu. Stefanenko, and Y.Yu. Sinin present scholarly treatments of specific periods or aspects of Zinoviev’s life and suggest that the time for a thoroughgoing re-evaluation of Zinoviev has arrived. [3] But, until now, English-language audiences have been limited to scarce academic articles on narrow topics. Egge has therefore rendered a distinct service to students of the Russian revolution and the early years of Soviet power. Relatively little is known of Zinoviev’s early life. He was born in 1883 to the family of a prosperous Jewish dairy farmer not far from Yelizavetgrad – later named Zinovievsk and then renamed Kirovsk for the man whose assassination in 1934 he was accused of abetting – in the Pale of Settlement in modern Ukraine. He was home schooled but, despite exposure to religious study (as evidenced by frequent biblical allusions in his speeches and writings), he gravitated to political radicalism. Like Trotsky, whose hometown was not far, he was drawn more to the internationalism of European Social Democracy than to Zionism or the Jewish Bund. After participating in study circles and strike organisations in the 1890s, young Radomyslsky joined the Russian Social-Democratic Labour Party in 1901. When his activities brought him to the attention of police, he left the country, eventually ending up in Switzerland, a haven for Russian political exiles. In Bern he enrolled in the university as a student of chemistry and soon met Zinaida (Zlata) Lilina, who became his first wife (and herself a prominent member of the RSDLP). Politics attracted him more than his studies, however, and it was not long before he met Vladimir Lenin, with whom he quickly established a steady working relationship. When the Bolsheviks and Mensheviks split at the second RSDLP congress in 1903, Zinoviev (who was not present at the congress) sided with Lenin. Together with Zlata, he joined the supporters of Lenin’s newspaper, Vperëd (“Forward”) in early 1905. From this point on Zinoviev became, according to Egge, Lenin’s ‘right-hand man’. Egge has reconstructed Zinoviev’s pre-revolutionary years from a wide array of sources, recounting Zinoviev’s friendship and collaboration with Lenin and Krupskaya during their time abroad, his participation in RSDLP congresses (beginning with the Fifth in 1907 in London at the age of 23), and his rise to prominence among the Bolshevik leadership in St. Petersburg, focusing much of his attention on work with the trade unions. He quickly distinguished himself as an effective agitator, despite (or perhaps because of) his unusually high voice, which some described as ‘feminine’. Even Trotsky, whose negative appraisals of Zinoviev have left a lasting imprint on the historiography, credited him with drawing the participants of the London congress back to the hall, at a moment when all were in the process of leaving, by making a speech that earned him a spot on the Central Committee (p. 20). Egge’s compilation of the facts of Zinoviev’s whereabouts and contributions in the period before 1917 are a much-needed addition to the literature. But, aside from the claim that Lenin and Zinoviev worked closely with one another in exile, what do we know of Zinoviev’s development as a revolutionary thinker? On this point, Egge struggles to gainsay the consensus that Zinoviev was little more than a mouthpiece for Lenin’s ideas. Students at the party school in Longjumeau, France, reportedly called him Lenin’s ‘errand boy’, the Mensheviks referred to him as ‘Lenin’s lapdog’, and even party leaders said that Zinoviev ‘followed Lenin as the thread follows the needle’ (p. 41). David Riazanov offered a contrasting view, praising Zinoviev as, aside from Lenin, ‘the party’s most learned man’, especially well versed in economics and sociology. But that report comes via Anatolii Lunacharsky, whose portrait of Zinoviev was written at the height of the latter’s power in the early 1920s. Egge does note instances of disagreement with Lenin, but these appear more as questions of degree rather than of principle. A close analysis of Zinoviev’s voluminous writings in exile would seem to be the logical way to explain the man’s intellectual evolution. Yet, for all his laudable skill at locating the details of Zinoviev’s life, Egge stops short of such a step. He does make extensive use of Zinoviev’s History of the Bolshevik Party , published in 1923, and refers to excerpts of Zinoviev’s reminiscences published in 1989. But, though the majority of volumes of his works that were published are filled with articles written for a wide array of newspapers, Egge devotes little or no space to them. Zinoviev was extraordinarily prolific, reputed to have published in as many as 150 different venues. A detailed comparison of Lenin and Zinoviev’s writings to identify differences of viewpoint would be a gargantuan task, and Egge was surely eager to complete his project. Nevertheless, Zinoviev’s claim that, between 1907 and 1917, ‘all of Vladimir Ilyich’s most important manuscripts passed through our hands until we came to an agreement’ (p. 39), raises the possibility that the influence may have been to some degree mutually reinforcing. As important, Zinoviev’s output reflects his own involvement in the political debates of the pre-1917 era. This was of enormous consequence to his later political behaviour. His outbursts and accusations against his foes in the 1920s read as though he was still struggling against the perceived Social-Democratic heresies of the pre-revolutionary years, which confused many less seasoned comrades and alienated him from many others. As concerns 1917, Egge has carefully culled the existing literature and published primary sources to offer a subtle reading of Zinoviev’s actions and decisions. Whereas Trotsky and others characterised Zinoviev as cowardly at moments such as those connected with the June demonstrations and the July Days, his infamous ‘betrayal’ in October with Lev Kamenev, and his effort to negotiate with for a coalition of socialist parties, Egge suggests that he was, in fact, consistent throughout the year, supporting the seizure of power by the soviets, the expropriation of land from landlords, and opposing the war and the Provisional Government along with the parties that supported them. He did waver in deciding whether to support the June demonstrations, concerned that they would provide the Provisional Government with a pretext for a crackdown—a back-and-forth that damaged his reputation with the rank-and-file in Petrograd. From that point forward, however, Egge argues that Zinoviev held steadily to a moderate line among the Bolsheviks, and his actions should hardly be interpreted as cowardly. As one of Lenin’s closest associates, he was an obvious target for arrest after the July Days. The decision to hide in Finland came at the urging of party members who feared that they might face execution if they stayed and were arrested as alleged German spies. Yet Zinoviev returned to Petrograd sooner than Lenin, travelling to speak at meetings across the city. It was Lenin, rather than Zinoviev, who shifted his position on the soviets. Having turned against the soviets in the summer for their moderation and cooperation with the Provisional Government, Lenin grew insistent on a seizure of power in the name of the soviets when the radicalism of the soviets grew in September and October, even if it meant rule by a single party. Zinoviev, Kamenev, and others were not convinced that the Bolsheviks were strong enough to withstand counterrevolutionary forces or that a Bolshevik revolution would enjoy the support of the international proletariat. They preferred the Party to take its chances with the Constituent Assembly, arguing that although the Bolsheviks would most likely end up in a minority, the resulting government would be both legitimate and could be dominated by a Bolshevik-Left SR bloc as leftist platforms gained in popularity. The story of their ‘strikebreaking’ before the October Revolution—publishing their dissent in advance of the uprising and thereby revealing Bolshevik intentions—is well known. But it is worth considering, as Egge does, that although the dissenters may have appeared weak-kneed at that decisive moment, their reasoning may have been more sober than that of the majority in the Central Committee. Moreover, Zinoviev showed determination in defying Lenin’s authority (and friendship) by sticking to his position (pp. 77-80). Despite Lenin’s blistering criticisms and calls for expulsion from the Party, he and Kamenev continued to negotiate with Socialist Revolutionaries and Mensheviks for a socialist coalition government and, together with three other members, they resigned their positions in the Central Committee. They only recanted their decisions to resign when it was clear that the dissidents had no support from the newly selected Central Committee, their negotiations had proved fruitless, and lower-ranking party members urged them to reverse their decisions in the name of party unity (p. 79). Egge appears to have conducted the bulk of his research in Moscow, so the chapters that cover Zinoviev’s leadership of Petrograd between 1918 and 1926 rely heavily on secondary literature and published documents. Nevertheless, he offers a solid account of Zinoviev’s time as ‘tsar’ (as he puts it) of the northern capital. Here, again, Egge balances much of the prevailing wisdom with a careful assessment of the actual political, economic, and social conditions in the city and surrounding territory. While he does take into account reports of Zinoviev indulging a taste for luxury amid the squalor and suffering of the civil war era—enjoying the use of several automobiles; moving first into the Astoria hotel and then into a large apartment; gaining weight even as most residents were tightening their belts—he is also clear about the enormous responsibilities Zinoviev assumed: chair of the presidium and executive committee of the Petrograd soviet; chair of the council of commissars of the Petrograd Labour Commune and the Northern Oblast; membership in the party’s Central Committee; and, eventually, chair of the Third International. Was Zinoviev an effective administrator? Egge’s assessment is mixed. He notes a tendency to mercurial temper, such as that which accompanied the calls for Red Terror against the new regime’s foes. Despite a relatively moderate attitude toward political opposition in mid-1918 (which earned him a harsh rebuke from Lenin), the assassination of the head of Petrograd’s political police (Cheka), Moisei Uritsky, prompted a sharp about-face. His sudden zeal for bloodshed embarrassed some of his close colleagues, a shift that some commentors attributed to cowardice and panic. Egge remains uncommitted, noting Samokhodkin’s diagnosis of ‘neurasthenia’ resulting from the childhood trauma as well as the possibility of shock following an alleged assassination attempt (p. 107). At the same time, Zinoviev played a crucial role in advocating for Petrograd. He opposed the relocation of the capital to Moscow in 1918; and, although he lost that battle, he nevertheless consistently fought to support the interests of workers and industry in the northwest, both of which had been devastated by years of war and revolution. Indeed, Zinoviev deliberately promoted the image of Petrograd as the cradle of the revolution and its workers and sailors as the vanguard of the entire Soviet working population. He was quick to use Lenin’s death in January 1924, to add lustre to the city by having it renamed Leningrad. He was jealous of his authority, yet he surrounded himself with capable lieutenants who ran the city more or less effectively during his many trips to Moscow, where he maintained an apartment in the Kremlin. Those trips increased as Zinoviev was drawn into political struggles after Lenin was gone. But, despite harsh judgments, such as that of Robert V. Daniels, that the Leningrad party organisation only backed Zinoviev in opposition in 1925, because he was ‘the undisputed boss in his own territory’, it is worth noting that many of the city’s party leaders and rank-and-file members maintained their loyalty to him into the late 1920s, well after it was clear that his defeat was complete. [4] Egge covers familiar terrain in recounting Zinoviev’s alliance with Stalin and Kamenev against Trotsky, followed by his turn against Stalin as his misgivings grew over the latter’s exercise of power and his intentions. Egge does, however, add to the existing literature by taking seriously Zinoviev’s views on the New Economic Policy (NEP) rather than portraying his positions solely as ‘power struggle’ politics. Whereas historians such as Daniels, Isaac Deutscher, and Robert C. Tucker emphasised Stalin’s theory of ‘socialism in one country’ primarily as a weapon in the battle against Trotsky, Egge elevates Zinoviev’s role in that debate. [5] Zinoviev was a longtime champion of world revolution as a foundational principle of Marxism and essential for Russia to overcome its backwardness by building socialism with the aid of more industrially developed countries to the west. The final failure of revolution in Germany in 1923 was deeply disappointing to the entire party; and it was a particular embarrassment to Zinoviev, who had staked much of his reputation on overly aggressive Comintern tactics there. But he continued to believe that world revolution was inevitable and necessary. A state policy that denied that necessity was un-Marxist and, when based on an economic policy that encouraged the enrichment of well-to-do peasants, it risked pushing Russia back towards capitalism. Egge’s approach broadens the context of the socialism-in-one-country debate and, thus, helps us understand more clearly Zinoviev and Kamenev’s opposition in late 1925, as well as their rapprochement with Trotsky in 1926. They could not agree with Trotsky on the theory of permanent revolution, but they did all see NEP as temporary or, as Zinoviev insisted, a ‘detour’, while Stalin and Bukharin were presenting it as the path to socialism. This framing also makes it easier to understand how Zinoviev could eventually retract his opposition once Stalin abandoned NEP in his assault on Bukharin, the Right Opposition, and pro-peasant policies generally. Egge does not deny the opportunism implicit in Zinoviev’s bowing before Stalin, but he does not characterise it as an act of cowardice. He shows that Zinoviev believed he could maintain a position of loyal opposition and, indeed, continued to correspond with former oppositionists for years. The violence of collectivisation exceeded anything that Trotsky, Zinoviev, or Kamenev would have endorsed, but at least the problem was now the specific policies of the person in charge rather than the Party’s overall policy direction. Egge’s first book, a study of the murder of Sergei Kirov (the event that ultimately led to Zinoviev’s trial and execution), provided much of the source material for his final chapters. [6] This is easily the strongest section of the biography. He has carefully sifted through Zinoviev’s collection in the Central Party Archive (RGASPI) and has uncovered detailed private correspondence and unpublished manuscripts that substantially expand what we know about the man’s final years. In his confinement, Zinoviev wrote a lengthy semi-autobiography entitled, ‘A Justified Sentence’ ( Zasluzhennyi prigovor ), in which he recounted his numerous sins and made a show of accepting the Party’s condemnation of him. Egge uses this source judiciously, given the circumstances under which it was written, but also fruitfully to fill many gaps in the story of his period as a pariah. From exile with Kamenev to Kaluga, back to Moscow, to Kazan, to imprisonment, Egge relates Zinoviev’s repeated attempts to return to political life, each time with greater desperation. Egge admits that we do not know the details of how Zinoviev met his death shortly after his trial in August 1936. He retells the well-known story of him grovelling and begging for his life, but, as he does consistently throughout the book, he points out the reasons for scepticism with the available accounts. Considering the many-sided image of Zinoviev that emerges in these pages, nearly any possibility is open. But Egge seems most persuaded that Zinoviev understood very well what awaited him and met his fate simply with resignation. This book is thorough and well researched. It has long been needed in the historiography of the Bolshevik revolution. Most of the details herein have been available for a long time, but, as the dissertations mentioned and a 2023 conference in St. Petersburg dedicated to Zinoviev suggest, interest in the man and his life has never been greater, and we owe Egge a debt of gratitude for providing what will surely be a standard account for some time. Yet the biography raises perhaps as many questions as it answers. What, after all, do we want to know about Grigory Zinoviev? Returning to Egge’s subtitle, we can accept that, at least in the years of exile abroad and up to the February revolution, Zinoviev had probably the closest working relationship with Lenin of any Bolshevik. It is not clear from Egge’s narrative, however, that he continued to be ‘Lenin’s right-hand man’ after their exile together in Finland. So, in what sense should we think of him as such? He was an effective agitator for Lenin’s positions at key moments, such as making the case for the Brest-Litovsk Treaty and the trade-union debate before the Tenth Party Congress. But did Lenin continue to rely on him as a sounding board for theoretical questions? Was Zinoviev an insightful interpreter of Lenin’s arguments? Does he deserve a re-evaluation as a Marxist theoretician in his own right? Egge does not venture a straightforward opinion on this point. Zinoviev wrote compulsively, yet much work remains for historians interested in giving his writings the attention they may actually deserve. What of Zinoviev’s reputation for instability, inconsistency, and cowardice? While Egge addresses the many weaknesses of the man’s character, readers hoping either for a full-throated rehabilitation or a thorough condemnation may be frustrated. But why is character more important in discussing Zinoviev than the other Bolshevik leaders? Perhaps it is because his downfall seems so dependent on his flaws. For Bolshevism’s foes, he conforms so easily to the archetype of a dogmatic yet craven villain that would-be rehabilitators find evidence of his shortcomings difficult to overcome. Unlike Nikolai Bukharin, Mikhail Tomsky, or Alexander Shlyapnikov, for example, whose biographers can portray their central figures—occasional circumstances notwithstanding—as basically sympathetic, Zinoviev seems to have had few likable qualities. [7] Zinoviev is also unlike Stalin or Nikolai Yezhov, whose biographers have little need or desire to rehabilitate their subjects, searching instead to explain their subjects’ particular evils. [8] Yet friends and foes of Lenin alike acknowledge his talent—so what did he see in Zinoviev that others have missed? Though Egge has commendably avoided clownish stereotypes, he has not brought us substantially closer to answering that question. To be fair, the question may, in the end, be unanswerable. Who can say what peculiar chemistry draws one person to another for collaboration and companionship? But, if we are to accept that Zinoviev was Lenin’s ‘right-hand man’, a more sustained assessment of their intellectual relationship is worth pursuing. Beyond questions of Zinoviev as a theorist, our picture of him as a practical leader could also use further elaboration. The in-fighting among the Central Committee members after Lenin’s death naturally draws our attention, but it is important to remember that Zinoviev held on to his responsibilities in what was, arguably, the most important industrial centre of the country until early 1926, even as he found himself drawn with greater frequency to Moscow. The late Alexander Rabinowitch has left us with a detailed analysis of the beginning of Zinoviev’s reign as ‘tsar’. [9] But St. Petersburg archives have much to tell us about the Zinoviev era there that historians such as myself have barely begun to examine. These comments should be understood as encouragement for further study rather than criticisms. Egge’s monograph advances our understanding of a key figure of the Bolshevik revolution well beyond the caricatures that have too long dominated the historiography. articles.title: One week after the earthquake in Colombia: figures, data, and controversies
articles.author: BreakThrough News
articles.content: It has been almost a week since Colombia, Panama, Venezuela, and Ecuador were jolted by a powerful earthquake . The epicenter of the August 10 earthquake was in San José del Palmar, in the Department of Chocó in Colombia, the country that has borne the brunt of the human and material losses. The earthquake measured 7.4 on the Richter scale and occurred at a depth of about 103 kilometers. More than 280 people died as a result of the natural disaster, and thousands of homes were destroyed. In total, the Unit for Risk and Disaster Management (UNGRD) reported 127,608 homes affected, 26,392 destroyed, and nearly 200 buildings collapsed, affecting nearly 120,671 families. The economic losses are also very high. According to some reports , total economic losses amount to about $9,570 million (nearly 2.1% of the South American country’s gross domestic product) illustrating the severity of the losses. The UNGRD also reported that more than 4,000 people were injured and that 194 are still missing, making it highly likely that the death toll will rise in the coming weeks. It was also reported that approximately 355 people have been rescued. Thousands of civilians, along with firefighters, members of the armed forces, police officers, and Colombian rescue teams, took to the streets to try to rescue as many people as possible. Typically, when natural disasters of this kind occur, various governments offer to send rescue teams and supplies to help better address the crisis. However, the government of right-wing President De la Espriella, who had been in office for only a few hours, decided to reject most of the offers to send rescue teams, stating that Colombia had enough experts to handle the crisis – a decision that sparked both diplomatic and domestic controversy. A few hours later, several members of the opposition speculated that the government actually only wanted assistance from governments aligned with its ideological stance, even though Foreign Minister Omar Bula himself said that was not the case. One of the critics was former presidential candidate Iván Cepeda, who argued that the aid the government accepts is “selective.” However, although aid has been accepted from dozens of countries, only search-and-rescue teams from four countries have been granted permission to operate in Colombia: Israel, the United States, Colombia, and El Salvador. The government stated that the selection criteria were based solely on technical considerations, although several critics have argued that this is actually a matter of ideological discretion that should carry little weight in times of emergency. Israeli forces in Colombia Among them, the group that has likely drawn the most attention is the 82 Israeli soldiers who have arrived to assist in search-and-rescue operations in central and southwestern Colombia. “We will be stationed at various points throughout the city, coordinating with local authorities to enter the collapsed areas and, God willing, find survivors during the rescue efforts,” said Ronny Kaplan, a spokesperson for the Israeli forces. Several opposition groups, including the Historic Pact, have criticized the presence of Israeli forces and have demanded clarification on “under what capacity they have come” – that is, whether as soldiers or as rescue workers – since, as Senator Cepeda stated, the Colombian Constitution requires the legislature to authorize the transit of foreign troops through Colombia, something that has not occurred. In this regard, former President Gustavo Petro said on X: “If the Israeli soldiers who arrived in Colombia brought weapons rather than medicine and rescue supplies, then we are facing a deception. This is a military occupation of Colombian territory without the permission of the Senate of the Republic.” These suspicions have been echoed by several social organizations, human rights advocates, and political leaders, who assert that Colombia does not need soldiers coming to provide technical and humanitarian assistance, but rather rescue workers of a different kind – such as those offered by several other countries. For now, various nations continue to send aid to Colombia. The United Nations has joined these efforts, promising food assistance for 100,000 people affected by the August 10 earthquake. Nils Grede, director of the World Food Program (WFP) in Colombia, said : “The solidarity shown immediately after the earthquake has been extraordinary … But we know from experience that recovery does not end when the initial wave of support subsides … We are committed to standing with the affected communities for as long as they need support.”

articles.title: Fujimori faces the first protests of her administration
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: A wave of protests and demonstrations have rocked diverse regions of Peru in recent days. The recently inaugurated right-wing President Keiko Fujimori is facing, very early on, the first protests of her term. Several transport workers’ groups have taken to the streets due to the rampant rise in fuel prices plaguing the entire region. They also decided to halt their activities and blocked several roads in protest against prices that, they claim, are impoverishing them. Prices have skyrocketed across Latin America due to the US-Israeli war on Iran. Furthermore, Peru is experiencing a serious domestic supply shortage that dates back to March of this year, particularly at the state-owned oil company Petroperú, which distributes a significant amount of diesel and gasoline to various regions of the country. These events, in a strongly neoliberal country, have caused diesel prices to double between February and August 2026, while the prices of other fuels have risen by 50%. One of the areas most affected by the protests is in the Peruvian Amazon, specifically in Ucayali, where several kilometers of roads have been blocked. In addition, clashes between protesters and police have been reported, resulting in the arrest of 11 civilians and injuries to five police officers. In response, the country’s president announced a temporary subsidy of up to 15% for “freight and passenger transport operators,” hoping this will ease the protesters’ demands and restore calm to the situation. According to Economy Minister Elmer Cuba, the subsidy will also include river transport operators and motorcycle taxi drivers. The measure, however, will last only three months and, as previously mentioned, will meet the demand of only a portion of the population. According to the government, it is estimated to lower prices by between 15 and 20%. Nevertheless, despite the promises and the signing of a memorandum of understanding between the government representative in the area, Manuel Gambini, and some union leaders, several groups of transport workers stated that they will continue with roadblocks and strikes because they consider the Fujimori administration’s measures to be “insufficient.” In light of this situation, some experts have pointed out that Fujimori’s measure is purely palliative and does not resolve the serious contradiction between a highly volatile pricing system and workers’ living conditions, which remain stagnant. Thus, if prices remain high after the three-month subsidy period, experts assert that there is a high likelihood that the cost of the crisis will be passed on to transportation service users, which could lead to even greater dissatisfaction and potential future protests. For now, Fujimori has stated that the transport workers’ demands are “fair” and has responded with a measure to calm tensions. In this way, she has gained some time and legitimacy in the face of protests that have “knocked on her door” barely a few days into her term. However, Peru’s economic model (clearly aligned with neoliberal orthodoxy) demonstrates just how fragile stability is for the most impoverished sectors once an internal cause (shortages) and/or an external cause (war in West Asia) shakes the markets. Faced with this, the Peruvian government has failed to find a satisfactory solution, leading to significant political instability that is often masked by partisan conflicts and crises involving political leaders.

articles.title: Argentina: The streets put a stop to Milei’s plundering
articles.author: Julian Bokser
articles.content: Javier Milei’s government recently suffered a double defeat. The first occurred in the streets, with massive protests against his plan to liberalize land purchases by foreigners. The second took place in the halls of the Argentine Congress, where he failed to secure enough votes to pass the bill as presented. Both defeats point to the same thing: a power project that is beginning to show the limits of its strength. The bill that the ruling party sought to impose, under the name “Law on the Inviolability of Private Property,” was neither an isolated initiative nor a simple regulatory adjustment. It was part of a broader series of attacks on national sovereignty: establishing mechanisms to accelerate the foreign ownership of land, facilitating external control over strategic resources, and clearing the way for Argentine territory, its common goods, and its decision-making authority over them to become increasingly subordinate to interests outside the country. Thousands of people took to the streets to protest this advance. The government responded as it always does when the people organize: with tear gas and rubber bullets, leaving people injured and detained. The repression was not an isolated excess. It is a method. Every time austerity measures encounter resistance, the state reveals its most violent face in an attempt to discipline those it cannot convince. Because that is what is beginning to crumble: hegemony, the ability to persuade. In the streets, one can feel the weariness in the face of economic austerity that punishes the popular majority while benefiting a handful of concentrated sectors. These austerity measures are neither a technical whim nor a deviation from a well-intentioned plan. They are the form that, in Argentina, a broader strategy of the international New Right takes to subjugate the peoples of the Global South: lowering wages, handing over natural resources, dismantling rights, and calling this plunder “modernization.” Milei does not manage this strategy from an autonomous position; he carries it out as an unconditional ally of a hyper-imperialism that is currently in a phase of decline and, for that very reason, is all the more dangerous: it needs to seize what remains of the Global South to sustain an order that can no longer guarantee well-being, not even in its own centers. In Congress, the other front, the government also failed to achieve its goals. Attempts to buy parliamentary support – to forge majorities through the offer of positions, promises, and pressure – fell short. It had to back down. First, on the core provisions of the misnamed “Law on the Inviolability of Private Property.” Then with the reform of the Fire Management Act, resigning itself to a scaled-back version. Two setbacks that expose the fragility of a project once believed to be unbeatable. The mobilization against foreign land ownership revealed something deeper than mere opposition to a specific law. It revealed a breaking point in the ruling class’s ability to build consensus around a social order that benefits only itself. That consensus, which for months seemed solid, began to crack. It remains to be seen how the anger that became visible in the rain, surrounding Congress, will be channeled into organized action. Vijay Prashad has been pointing out from the Tricontinental Institute that the current cycle of global capitalism offers no solutions within its own rules: the crisis is managed by shifting its costs to the Global South, while local bourgeoisies (now junior partners in that system) apply domestically the prescriptions that international finance capital designs abroad. Prashad insists that no austerity measure of this kind can be sustained without a parallel cultural battle, aimed at presenting as inevitable what is, in reality, a political choice serving specific interests. When that cultural battle begins to lose ground (as happened in Argentina) a rift opens that no amount of repression can fully close. A glimpse of this was seen in the banner passed around repeatedly by thousands in the crowd—the same one the national team players unfurled after their victory over England in the last World Cup – bearing the slogan “The Malvinas are Argentine.” Since the Malvinas War in 1982, that match has been anything but just another game. The 1986 match, just a few years after the war, was unforgettable: it was the match of the ‘Hand of God’ and the greatest goal in history, both scored by Diego Maradona. Football carries the burden of the claim to the Malvinas Islands, now a NATO base under British control and a platform for the plundering of oil and other common resources of the South Atlantic. That flag struck a chord with the Argentine people – the chord of a sovereignty never fully relinquished, not even when the ruling power insists on negotiating it away. But no single chord, on its own, is enough to change the course of a country. The anger seen in the streets needs to be organized, channeled, and transformed into a concrete plan. Otherwise, it runs the risk of burning out in the very intensity of the moment, of dissipating into frustration as soon as the tide of mobilization recedes. The task at hand, then, is not merely to resist the next onslaught. It is to build the political force capable of sustaining over time what the streets demonstrated amid the storm: that there is a limit, that this limit must be defended, and that the homeland is not for sale.
